column1: # surfaces.tsv (harbor#950) — every surface a name is rendered on, and how (standards/naming.md §6.1).
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. One tuple of terms gives every surface its name, so the renderer per
# surface is the grammar's other half. Before this file it was a table in prose that the lint
# could not read; the naming guide is now generated from these rows (`--gen naming-guide`), and
# every example below runs as a pass fixture in `bin/lint-name.sh --self-test`, so an example the
# COLUMNS  id <TAB> renderer <TAB> family <TAB> checked <TAB> example <TAB> rule <TAB> view <TAB> note
#   id        the surface id that `bin/lint-name.sh --check <surface> <name>` takes
#   renderer  a GRAMMAR when `rule` is set, prose otherwise. The lint parses a name back through it
#             and renders a tuple with it (`--parse`, `--render`), so editing the cell changes the
#             verdict. <slot> is one word group, [..] is optional, anything else is literal, and a
#             slot spelled in capitals renders in capitals. Slots: <family> <verb> <system> (or
#             <REPO>) are registered terms; <family-or-domain> is a family or a domain; <object>
#             <subject> <aspect> <name> <id> <ext> are free. The joiner inside a slot is _ when the
#   family    required | optional | -   whether the first word must be a family (or a domain)
#   checked   tree     lint-name.sh scans the repo tree for it, and --check accepts it
#             check    --check accepts it; nothing in a repo tree carries it
#             no       not machine-checked here: another tool, or review only (the note says which)
#   example   a name that MUST pass; - when the surface is not checked, or when the thing checked is
#             a directory on disk and its examples are the fixtures (repo-kind). Every example whose
#             `rule` is set must also survive parse then render unchanged (--self-test)
#   rule      the rules id that reports a name the grammar does not parse or whose slot is not
#             the registered term it needs; - when the renderer is prose, not a grammar
#   view      - when the surface is judged by its own code. Otherwise <surface>[:<rule>,<rule>]: this
#             id is another surface under a second name (`path.test` is `test`), or that surface
#             judged for the listed rules only (`case` is `path` reporting name.case alone). The
#             target is a row of this file and each rule a row of controls.tsv; a view is never of a view
